output:
**What I found:** Finance wants to cut the CI runner pool from 10 to 8. Refuse the cut and the fallback split (the record calls this Reject), because 8 runners would have to absorb the same 7.8 runners' worth of work and run at 97.5% utilization.

**Why it matters:** At 78% utilization, jobs already wait 9 minutes on average and 31 minutes in the afternoon. At 97.5%, the skill's queueing rule of thumb (wait ∝ ρ/(1−ρ)) puts average wait at about 11× today's, and the afternoon peak can need more than 8 runners, so its queue may keep growing until merges ease off. Splitting the pool adds a routing table and two queues, and nobody has measured whether it shortens wait at all.

**Do this first:**
1. Pull hourly runner utilization and queue wait for the last 30 days from the CI runner metrics, so the 14:00–17:00 peak has a measured number.
   - Follow-up: test whether spreading out the afternoon merges lowers the 31-minute peak wait before anyone buys or removes runners.

**What I did not check:**
- Hourly utilization at the peak (CI runner metrics export, broken out by hour).
- Variance in job duration, which also drives queue time (job duration distribution from the same 30-day data).
- Runner cost compared with the cost of developers waiting (finance's per-runner cost × the change in wait-hours).

```
Scope:          Shared CI runner pool, 10 runners, last 30 days
Constraint:     Runner pool during 14:00–17:00 (31 min wait vs 12 min job, so wait > job time);
                root cause is Mura: merges bunch up in the afternoon. Peak utilization: Not measured
Decision:       Reject (cut to 8); Reject (3+7 split as proposed)
Flow signal:    ρ = 0.78 now → 0.975 with 8 runners (7.8 runners' worth of work / 8).
                Kingman factor ρ/(1−ρ): 3.5 → 39, ≈11× average wait. Peak load is above
                average, so the afternoon queue at 8 runners is likely to grow without limit.
                The 22% "idle" is the headroom that keeps today's wait at 9 min
Evidence:       User-supplied 30-day figures: 78% avg utilization, 12 min job, 9 min avg wait,
                31 min peak wait, steady daily job count
Next action:    Measure hourly utilization; trial spreading the afternoon merges (a policy change,
                not capacity) and re-measure peak wait
Verification:   Not run. Analysis only; no CI data accessed
Residual risk:  Job duration variance and peak ρ unknown. A split pool could cut wait for the
                small repositories while raising it for the 7-runner pool. Unmeasured either way
```

Cut the pool: no

The split adds a routing table, a second lane, and a repository-to-lane mapping that has to be kept up to date. That makes the system more complex on three of the four complexity axes the litmus test uses (D, K and n), and nobody has measured any improvement in flow. As proposed, it fails the skill's test for an optimization. Queueing theory also predicts that splitting one pool into two dedicated lanes raises total wait for the same capacity.

Litmus test: fail
